主要内容: President Donald Trump, who has called himself the 'King of Debt,' has expressed a desire to wipe out Puerto Rico's debt, but experts say this is unlikely. Bond strategists indicate that Congress has already initiated a restructuring process, and it is improbable that this will be altered. While Trump's focus on the island may result in additional government loans, these would likely carry more weight than existing debt. Puerto Rico's bonds experienced a sharp decline following Trump's comments, with the benchmark general obligation bonds trading at 36 cents on the dollar. Bondholders, already anticipating a restructuring of the $72 billion debt, may now face an even larger loss. Congress has allocated some funds for Puerto Rico as part of hurricane relief, and the White House has requested more. Puerto Rico's current debt-to-GDP ratio is about 68 percent, compared to the average of 17 percent for U.S. states. The restructuring process is moving through the Title 3 bankruptcy framework, which was approved by Congress. Experts believe the restructuring may take several years due to the complexity of the situation and the impact of Hurricane Maria on the island's economy. Trump cannot completely wipe away Puerto Rico's debt, as the commonwealth constitution clearly states that bondholders must be paid first, even before pension beneficiaries. Some strategists believe Congress would not have much appetite to remove Puerto Rico's obligations, even if Trump wanted to. Approximately 25 percent of the island's general obligation bonds are insured, as are 70 percent of its COFINA sales tax bonds. The stocks of bond insurance companies, such as MBIA, were under pressure, with MBIA down about 9 percent. Strategists noted that it's not just hedge funds that will be affected by a haircut, as the majority of debt holders are individuals and mutual funds. Trump did not acknowledge individual holders in his comments on the debt. Lipton pointed out that White House Budget Director Mick Mulvaney emphasized that Trump's comments should not be taken literally, and the federal government will not bail out the debt.
